analysis.one_liner: Cuts the federal corporate tax rate to a 20 percent top rate.
analysis.headline: The bill was never taken up in the Senate Finance Committee and received no cosponsors; it died at the end of the 113th Congress without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the corporate income tax so that corporations pay 15 percent on their first $50,000 of taxable income and 20 percent on everything above that. That is a large cut from the 35 percent top rate then in law, and it applies to all corporations, including professional firms like law and accounting corporations. The bill had no offsetting provisions to make up the lost revenue. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and their shareholders would gain the most. A company with $1 million in taxable income would pay roughly $195,000 instead of $340,000 under the rate structure then in law — a tax cut of about 40 percent at higher income levels. Law firms, consulting firms, and other companies organized as personal service corporations would get the same cut, which they generally do not receive in other corporate rate-cut proposals.

how_it_helps.text: Reduces the top corporate tax rate from 35 percent to 20 percent on income above $50,000, with 15 percent on income below that [S2][S3].
Applies the lower rate to personal service corporations — firms such as law, accounting, and consulting practices that are taxed as corporations — rather than excluding them [S2].
Supporters of corporate rate cuts argue the existing 35 percent rate encourages companies to book profits overseas; the bill's title frames the cut as restoring American competitiveness [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Someone would have to make up the lost federal revenue. The bill contains no offsetting tax increases or spending cuts, so if enacted the shortfall would eventually be absorbed through more federal borrowing, future tax increases, or spending cuts. Programs that corporations currently help fund through the corporate tax — military spending, public services, and social programs — would compete for a smaller pool of revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no pay-fors: it cuts the corporate rate with no accompanying tax increases or spending offsets, so every dollar of the cut adds to federal deficits or debt unless later replaced [S3].

Small businesses organized as corporations get the same 15 percent rate on their first $50,000, but the flat 20 percent rate above that removes the current graduated rates (which step down to 15 percent for income up to $50,000 and 25 percent up to $75,000), raising the marginal rate for the smallest profitable corporations at the bottom bracket's upper edge [S3].

A good-faith objection to any rate cut at this scale is that it permanently shrinks the part of the tax code borne most directly by shareholders — who skew toward higher-income households — while the revenue loss lands on the general budget that funds services used by everyone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a large, permanent tax cut to corporations with no way to pay for it in the bill itself. The rate reduction is real and, at the higher income levels, cuts corporate tax bills by roughly 40 percent. The cost is a roughly equivalent revenue loss for the federal government, which would show up as more debt or pressure on other taxes and programs. There is no mechanism in the bill — no revenue floor, no clawback, no expiry — to balance those two things, so the weighing comes down almost entirely to whether one believes the rate cut would pay for itself through growth, a claim the bill text and summary do not address.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and sat there with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Johanns of Nebraska introduced the bill on January 24, 2013 [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; that referral was the last action ever taken on the bill [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill received no markup, hearing, or floor vote before the 113th Congress expired on January 3, 2015, at which point it lapsed [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, corporate tax rates stayed unchanged and the revenue those rates raise was preserved for the federal budget. Shareholders and corporations gained nothing, and no one outside the sponsor signed on to the effort.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply lapsed.

for.name: Mike Johanns
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on January 24, 2013; recruited no cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican senator sponsored the bill and no members of either party cosponsored it; opposition was not so much active as the absence of any support beyond the sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would have cut the top corporate rate from 35 percent to 20 percent with no revenue offsets. The cost of that cut would fall on the general federal budget, meaning other taxpayers or public programs would eventually absorb it.

industries.industry: Professional service firms (law, accounting, consulting) organized as corporations
industries.note: The bill explicitly includes personal service corporations in the low rate, which most corporate tax proposals exclude. These firms would get the same roughly 40 percent cut on higher income.

They would pay 15 percent on their first $50,000 of income, but lose the existing graduated brackets above that level and pay a flat 20 percent, so the smallest profitable corporations would see both cuts and increases depending on income.
